item.content: {"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=long-term+convergence+properties+of+path-dependent+preference+models+reinforcement+learning&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.1109/ictc66702.2025.11388608\", \"title\": [\"Reinforcement Learning-Based Correction of Indoor Path Loss Models for Wi-SUN Sub-GHz Communications\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1109/ictc66702.2025.11388608\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 10, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7528788\", \"title\": [\"Solution Methods for Long-Term Debt Default Models: Convergence and Accuracy\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Long-term-debt default models are the workhorse of quantitative sovereign-debt research, yet the methods used to solve them have never been held to a common standard of accuracy. The difficulty is economic: the option to default makes the borrower&apos;s problem non-concave, and long maturities make the bond price a fixed point that feeds policy errors back into prices. We compare extreme-value taste shocks on a discrete menu with interpolated continuous-choice optimization in the Chatterjee and Eyigungor (2012) one-asset model and the Bianchi, Hatchondo and Martinez (2018) reserves model, both validated against the published replication outputs. First, smoothing the choice rule distorts primarily portfolio composition rather than leverage: reserves vary sharply with the taste-shock scale while mean debt barely moves—an error a one-asset model cannot exhibit. Second, convergence and accuracy are distinct. Borrower Euler residuals, lender pricing residuals, and a global menu-deviation audit reveal converged solutions that violate the model’s optimality conditions, a non-converged terminal iterate that matches converged candidates on the scored conditions, and matched moments—the literature’s usual check—that mask an order of magnitude in first-order accuracy. Third, taste shocks solve the portfolio model roughly three to four times faster than the continuous-choice reference at a small welfare cost, and a single post-solve re-optimization of the actions, repriced and re-evaluated, eliminates the measured welfare gap with the reference. An exact factorization of the pricing recursion contributes to the implementation’s speed.</jats:p>\",…
